Parashas Tetzaveh | Feb 12th 2022

“Dear Brother, Hold On” 

Rabbi David Yisrael Kalmus

In the beginning of Parashat Tetzaveh, HaShem instructs Moshe to encourage the Jewish People to bring to him “pure, pressed olive oil for lighting” (Shemot 27:20). All the pristine oil that Moshe gathered would then be used to illuminate the Menorah in the form of a “ner tamid,” a perpetual lighting. This unique luminary in the Mishkan would serve as the model and prototype for the beacon of light which would shine forth from the Beit HaMikdash to the entire world (Menachot 86B). 

Paradoxically, the process of unearthing this potent, ethereal light begins with tremendous pressure and weight placed on the physical olives themselves. Through intense duress alone, the olives then give birth to a wondrous oil capable of brilliant illumination. 

This entire paradigm alludes to the deep, internal process of a Jewish person drawing out the inner light stored within him or herself in order to provide illumination for those all around, and in turn, becoming a “light unto the nations” (Yeshaya 49:6). The goal and destination of a Jew is certainly wondrous, but the path to lighting up one’s brethren is nonetheless preceded by an intense experience of being “katit,” crushed. 

As Chazal famously teach, “Why are the Jews compared to olives? The olive sits upon its branch. It is plucked, squeezed, ground, and crushed, and only then does it give its oil. So too, when the Jews endure suffering, they show their mettle” (Shemot Rabbat 36:1). What allows a person the strength and inner fortitude to endure such intense trials and tribulations on their journey to fulfilling their unique potential? 

In my favorite lesson of Likutey Moharan known in Breslov circles as “The Rebbe’s Letter,” Rebbe Nachman unusually and quite forwardly addresses his students, both in the present and to us now in the future, in the first person. The lesson is reminiscent of a letter written to a dear friend. Here, Rebbe Nachman exhorts each and every one of us in our uniquely challenging path towards actualizing one’s innermost self with these potent words, “When a person begins serving HaShem, the way is that they show him rejection. It seems as if HaShem is completely ignoring him and not turning to him at all because HaShem does not want him at all.

A person needs to be very stubborn, encouraging himself very, very much and paying no attention whatsoever to all this, for in truth, all distancing is nothing but being brought near. A person needs tremendous determination to be strong and courageous, to hold on and maintain his position even if they cause him to fall time and again. This is because one must surely experience all these falls, descents, confusions, and so on before entering the gates of holiness. The True Tzaddikim underwent all this. And so we heard from a True Tzaddik who said: “Had anyone, no matter whom, told me when I first began serving HaShem: “Brother! Be strong and hold on!” I would have run very quick in serving HaShem. For (that Tzaddik) too, experienced all the aforementioned, yet did not hear any encouragement, from anybody. Remember this well! Give yourself much encouragement, and do what you can in serving HaShem. Then, with the accruement of days and years, with HaShem’s help, you will surely enter into the gates of holiness. For HaShem is full of compassion and wants you very much. And so the rule my beloved brother, is to be very strong and courageous” (Likutey Moharan Tinyana, 48). 

The True Tzaddik whom Rebbe Nachman is mysteriously alluding to appears to be himself. But the open ended nature of Rebbe Nachman’s disclaimer lends itself to interpreting these very words to ourselves as well. This is supported by the fact that Rebbe Nachman strongly asserted that anyone who had the courage to be his faithful disciple, without veering even the slightest bit from his established path, would become a great Tzaddik in his own right, come what may (Chayei Moharan, 320). 

Over the course of my years since becoming Ba’al Teshuva and, with HaShem’s compassion, ultimately finding the Rebbe who so deeply resonated with the root of my soul, I have repeatedly drawn tremendous encouragement and inspiration from this letter. Continuously overcoming debilitating mental health conditions and psycho-spiritual vulnerabilities in order to provide light to my family and friends around me has proven to be the most formidable task of my life. And yet, the oil which has been produced by the constant “crushing,” has become a blazing fire of hope and consolation for those around me. This is my pride and joy in both this world and the next. All of this is in merit of my “Moshe Rabbeinu,” the Tzaddik Yesod Olam, Rebbe Nachman, from whom all this oil has been excavated by and gathered to. 

I know I have stated this many times. But I will continue to do so, because this point requires constant encouragement. Do not ever give up. If you fall down, force yourself with whatever means necessary to dust yourself off and get back up again. Even if you fall many times throughout a day, find the courage to start over again. And even if you feel that you are alone in your struggles, you must know that I am over here fighting the very same fight with you. 

And remember, each time you force yourself to begin anew, you are drawing out more and more pure oil. It is this sacred oil which will serve as the primary source of light in the final Beit HaMikdash, a brilliant luminance which will light up the whole world. A real and everlasting “ner tamid.” In the meantime, my dear brother, hold on. 

Shabbat Shalom. 

Parashas Terumah | Feb 5th 29nd 2022

Terumah of a Broken Heart

Aaron S. London

There is a beautiful moment in Torah סה where Rebbe Nachman describes the existence of a supernal field. And, in this field, the most gorgeous trees and vegetation grow. So much so, that the Rebbe says that it is impossible to describe the beauty of this field. He explains that the trees and vegetation are really the holy souls of the Jewish people. As Rabbi Chaim Kramer elucidates in the English commentary to this Torah, this supernal field is the expression of the Shechinah Itself (Likutey Moharan, Volume 8, p. 2). 

However, there are many “naked souls” who roam outside the perimeter of this field. These souls, in their spiritual impoverishment, are not allowed to enter and their deepest yearning is to return to the .שדה 

The above synopsis is only a glimpse into the first section of a profound Torah with many facets to it. And, in truth, my words are coarse in comparison to the beauty that exists on those pages in sefer Likutey Moharan. 

Nonetheless, it is with this introduction, I would like to begin. 

When I heard Rav Moshe Weinberger share this Torah, I believe he characterized the field that Rebbe Nachman talks about as Hashem’s garden. How often do we feel like those naked souls wandering outside Hashem’s garden? 

Our trail through life can feel thick with brush and, as we trudge forward, contending with the realities of our physical existence, our eyes grow weary. In our weariness, the Echad that we declare everyday becomes blurry and we descend into the fragmented shards of our lives, confused and in pain. 

How can we get back to this garden? How can we return to the Echad? Of course, Rebbe Nachman presents a paradigm shifting answer in the Torah itself. 

Indeed, I would like to offer an insight that is in harmony with the tzaddik’s explanation, but through the lens of this week’s parashah. 

Parashas Terumah begins, “Hashem spoke to Moshe: Speak to the Children of Israel and let them take for Me a donation, from every man whose heart motivates him you shall take My donation” (25:1-2). The Torah continues and proceeds to list out the different materials that can be donated for the construction of the Mishkan. Then, in verse eight, the Torah famously writes, “They shall make a Sanctuary for Me so that I may dwell among them.” 

We know that, on the level of penimiyus, the construction of the physical Mishkan can be compared to the construction of the spiritual Mishkan that exists within the privacy of our own inner worlds. And I hearken back to the words of Rav Weinberger on Tisha B’Av two years ago when he describes how is it possible to raise up our hearts to Hashem when our hearts have become as hard as stone? And, based on a moshel that Rebbe Nachman gives, Rav Weinberger explains that the only way to offer a heart of stone to Hashem is to take a hammer and smash the heart into pieces. Now, with trembling hands, we can lift up those shards to Hashem Himself. 

What is the gold, silver, and copper of my inner world? What is the turquoise, purple, and scarlet wool of the heart? What are the materials of my internality that I am offering to Hashem? 

I would like to propose the materials of the inner Mishkan, so to speak, are the shards of that broken heart. 

When a person closes the door of his closet and sits in the darkness with his back bent over and says in hisbodedus, “Hashem, here it is: my pain and my humanity, my good and my bad, my love and my fear, my tears 

and my laughs – I offer them up to You. Every ripple of my life comes from You and even though I intellectually know that to be true, help me to feel that truth in my heart.” 

And, it is through the shaking voice of a Jew searching for his Creator, seeking the Echad in his life, that the heart begins to break. With those very rubbles, then “[t]hey shall make a Sanctuary for Me…” 

My dear friends, with the help of the Almighty, may we speak to Hashem in truth and enter the garden again with the terumah of our broken hearts. 

Gut Shabbos, 

Aryeah Leib Yishaya 

Parashas Mishpatim | Jan 29nd 2022

The End is Wedged in the Beginning

Rabbi David Yisrael Kalmus

In any completed process, there are two main components. These components are not at all the same, but they are undoubtedly equal. The first component is the beginning, and this reflects unlimited potential. The second component is the end, reflected by actualized reality (Aryeh Kaplan, Inner Space). 

According to Kabbalah, the beginning of any process is rooted in the spiritual quality of “Zachar,” maleness. The finality of any process is rooted in the spiritual quality of “Nekeva,” femaleness (AriZal, Etz Chaim). And just as the beginning lacks meaning without the end, so too the end does not take effect without the beginning. 

From here we can extract a basic principle of the Torah. Men and women are unequivocally equal. Despite superficial perception to the contrary, the intrinsic differences associated with both masculinity and femininity from the perspective of the Torah do not in any way undermine their deep rooted equality. In fact, their inherent differences actually serve to enhance, perfect, and complete the properties of the other. The Sages elucidate this point explicitly. 

Commenting on the first verse in this week’s Torah Portion, “And these are the laws that you must place before them” (Shemot 21:1), our Sages taught: The words “before them” indicate that in regard to all Torah laws, woman is equated with man (Kiddushin 35A). And while this is certainly referring to men and women in the simple sense, “man” and “woman” can also refer to two different types of essential spiritual service. 

“Man” corresponds to the intensive learning of Torah and “Woman” corresponds to authentic Tefillah, heartfelt prayer (Likutey Moharan 10). Rebbe Nachman teaches that as long as we do not make a balanced space for the existence of both forms of service in our own lives, than our individual and collective redemption will continue to allude us (Likutey Moharan 7). This is the secret of the halachah in the Shulchan Aruch which states that it is good for a person pray in the same place that he learns (Shulchan Aruch, (90:18). 

Over my half decade of teaching Torah, I have noticed the lack of harmony between these two essential elements in almost ever person I encounter. One person spends the majority of his day learning Torah, but privately feels very far from an authentic relationship with the One who created him- for “It is not good for man to be alone” (Bereshis 2:18). Another person spends countless hours in secluded meditation in the field pouring his heart out to HaShem Mitberach, but finds that he lacks true clarity and understanding. For the female dimension, Tefillah, “has no light of her own” (Zohar Bereshis 41). 

It personally took me quite some time to allow myself the permission to give equal time and energy into both. When I first became Ba’al Teshuva, I immersed myself in learning everything I could find, but did not actually experience HaShem in my life in a palpable way. I transitioned to speaking to HaShem at every chance I could get in Hitbodedut, but ultimately found that I came out feeling even more confused and heavier than when I began. 

The reason is very simple. Torah and Tefillah are both equal, and most importantly, synergetic (Likutey Moharan 2). Rebbe Nachman explains that it is the Torah that one learns that allows his Tefillot to get answered (Likutey Moharan 1). On the other hand, it is Tefillah which nurtures and waters one’s Torah learning, allowing one to achieve ever increasing levels of G-d consciousness (Likutey Moharan 8). 

Torah and Tefillah are not two separate entities living in a vacuum. They are two sides to a double edged sword, and it only with this fully loaded weapon that one can overcome all the challenges one has to face in this world, while simultaneously achieving the greatest level of closeness to HaShem (Likutey Moharan 2). 

I highly encourage anyone reading this to honestly assess the unspoken value they have placed on either Torah learning or heartfelt Tefillah in their lives. If you find that over the course of time, you have marginalized one of these practices for the sake of the other, then reassess. Because men and women were created equal. And without making a legitimate effort to equalize these two powerful forces in one’s life, the possibility for leaving one’s personal exile will always remain elusive. 

The Rebbe concluded, “The Mitnagdim argue that Torah study is a Jew’s main devotion. The Chassidim argue that prayer is the main devotion. But I say “Pray, learn, pray” (Avenha Barzel 10)! 

Shabbat Shalom. 

Our Beautiful Debt 

Aaron S. London, RN, BSN

Reb Noson shares with us important insights into avodas Hashem based on a pasuk found in this week’s parashah. The pasuk reads as follows: “When you lend money to My people, to the poor person [who is] with you, you shall not behave toward him as a lender; you shall not impose interest upon him.…” (22:24, translation from Chabad.org). 

Reb Noson offers a novel reading of this pasuk by demonstrating that the pasuk is also referring to the way Hashem relates to the Jewish people. He explains how, in truth, it would be fitting for Hashem to return the world to “tohu v’vohu” given our many sins. Nevertheless, Hashem sustains us only with His chesed in the aspect of a “loan,” where Hashem does not exact payment from us immediately, but rather is constantly extending the “deadline” of payment in order that we return and pay Hashem for the debts we owe through the sins we have committed. 

What emerges from Reb Noson’s understanding of the text are ideas that can energize and transform the way in which we approach our service of G-d. First and foremost, Reb Noson encourages us to see every moment of our lives, not as a right, but rather as a debt that we owe Hashem. 

As Rav Shlomo Wolbe eludicates in Pirkey Kinyon Daas, Preface Beis, where he describes how every person needs to consider – how am I obligated to conduct myself in each moment? The attitude is one of perceiving responsibility as the essential mode of experience, rather than entitlement. Therefore, an important shift in mindset occurs when a person understands that nothing is truly a given in his or her life. On the contract, every movement, every gesture, every breath is a gift from Above. 

What are these “debts” that we owe Hashem? Reb Noson makes it a point to convey that our “debts” specifically come out of our sins. Rabbi Chaim Miller, in his translation and elucidation of Sefer HaTanya entitled Practical Tanya, explains that “evil… means a blocking of G-d consciousness” (p. 94). In other words, when a person sins, he or she is committing an act – either in thought, word, or action – that severs oneself from awareness of the Divine, ultimately leading to some form of fallenness. 

Perhaps, then, one understanding of the repayment of the debt is a person’s ability to re-anchor oneself within G-d consciousness. Said differently, one’s responsibility to the moment is to energize the moment with the awareness that this experience comes directly from Hashem. In so doing, we “upgrade our consciousness” as my teacher, Rav Gerzi, so often explains and return those “fallen sparks” to their Source. 

However, there is a further point. Reb Noson writes that Hashem is constantly extending the deadline of payment. Why? Ultimately, because Hashem believes in our ability to pay back our debts. Hashem believes in our ability to believe in Him. As we say everyday in davening, Hashem “maintains His faith to those asleep in the dust” (Artscroll translation). 

No doubt, in these final moments before Mashiach, we are marred by the dirt of this world. Nevertheless, Hashem has emunah in our capacity to wipe the dust from our eyes and see how everything is truly from Him. 

הלכות העושה שליח לגבות חוב ב, אות כב לפי אוצר היראה) (צדקה סח 

Gut Shabbos.

Parashas Yisro | Jan 22nd 2022

Climb! But Hold Yourself

Rabbi David Yisrael Kalmus

In the Rambam’s magnum opus, Mishneh Torah, it is brought down that while it is a Mitzvah from the Torah to learn both by day and by night, nonetheless the majority of a person’s wisdom is acquired at night time. The Rambam subsequently adds that “anyone who desires the Crown of Torah should be careful to learn all of his nights, and not to lose out on even one moment from then” (Sefer HaMadah, Talmud Torah, 3:13). Rav Yosef Karo, in his preeminent work on the codification of Jewish Law, states that “a person needs to be vigilant to learn at night more so than during the day” (Shulchan Aruch, OC, 238). In the Gemara, Reish Lakish teaches that anyone who occupies himself with Torah at night, HaShem draws upon him a thread of love during the day (Chagigah 13B). 

Why do all the Sages emphatically encourage the learning of Torah and the cultivation of higher wisdom by night time, in contrast to the day? Furthermore, Breslov Chassidim sing out 

with tremendous fervor, “Kumi Roni V’Lailah,” – “Arise, sing out in the night” (Eichah, 2:19)! Why not sing during the day? Why only cry out the sweet melody of Torah at night? Rav Natan, the main disciple of Rebbe Nachman, provides elucidation to this mystery. 

It states in this week’s Torah Portion, Parashat Yitro, that prior to receiving the Torah on Har Sinai, the Jews first “journeyed” and “came to the desert” (Yitro, 19:2). Rav Natan elucidates that the nature of the “desert” is that it is inherently inhospitable, devoid of comfort and full of dangers to life, a place seemingly bereft of G-dliness (Likutey Halachot VII, 51A). The Zohar HaKadosh states unequivocally that the “desert” is the domain of the “sitra achra,” the place of negative spiritual forces (Zohar, Tetzaveh 184A). 

On paper, this would appear to be the last place to draw profound insights and higher consciousness. Paradoxically, Rav Natan states that the primary Torah that a person attains is that which he acquires in the “desert,” with struggle and with difficulty (Likutey Halachot III, 205A). 

Why does concealment and confusion breed wisdom? Why should intense struggle promote an uptick in genuine understanding? 

The answer is that suffering, otherwise known as “night-time,” cultivates humility. 

Har Sinai is the smallest of all mountains, the ultimate symbol of humility (Sotah 5A). Moshe Rabbienu, the transmitter of the Torah, was “extremely humble, more than any person on the face of the earth” (Behalotcha, 12:3). G-d consciousness can only be grasped through humility because the truth, like HaShem Himself, is Infinite. 

How does someone who is finite grasp something which transcends the limitations of the physical world? Only through “bitul,” the nullification of ego and lower self. By being stripped of one’s physical powers and intellectual prowess, man can make a space for the One who has no shape or image. Before this, there is no genuine vessel to receive the Infinite Light. 

The Sages teach that the the place in which Klal Yisrael originally received the Torah, “Sinai,” has the same numerical value as “Sulam,” a ladder (Midrash Rabba, 68:12). The reason Sinai is a “ladder,” is because it is only through attainment of genuine humility that one can ascend to spiritual heights (Likutey Halachot VIII, 259A). 

I encourage everyone to take a moment over Shabbat to allow themselves the space and vulnerability to contemplate the blessing of their own personal “night-time.” However challenging it might have been, or even continues to be, know that the humility which it engenders ultimately provides the ladder through which we can receive the greatest blessing of all, the truth. And in the end, it is only through truth that the Redemption takes place (Sefer HaMiddot, Emet, 9B). 

Shabbat Shalom 

Letters that Shine, Souls that Sparkle

Aaron S. London, RN, BSN

In sefer Likutey Halachos, Reb Noson draws a fascinating distinction between Rebbe Akiva’s students perishing in between Pesach and Shevuos and Klal Yisrael receiving the Torah at Har Sinai. Reb Noson explains how the talmidei Rebbe Akiva needed to share with the world the Torah they received from their teacher. However, because they lacked love and kinship amongst themselves, they blemished their capacity to express Torah. Reb Noson writes, “… they needed to draw down Torah and to fix the restrictions and vessels that would merit all of the Jewish people to receive the light of Hashem properly. Because through each letter, word, and section of the Torah HaKedosha and through each and every halachah, vessels and restrictions are made to receive the light of Hashem, and reveal His blessed kingship in the world” (p. 432, Volume II). 

In other words, the aleph-beis itself becomes the basic means through which the tzaddikim give us access to the light of G dliness. Yet, in regards to the talmidei Rebbe Akiva, their lack of ahavah for each other compromised their capacity to construct these “vessels of expression” – i.e. the very letters themselves – through which Klal Yisrael can reach Ohr HaEin Sof. As a result, the talmidim of Rebbe Akiva perished. 

In contradistinction, the pasuk in this week’s parashah writes, “… and Israel encamped there opposite the mountain” (19:2). Rashi comments and explains that the pasuk is coming to teach us that Klal Yisrael was unified – “like one man with one heart.” Reb Noson expands upon Rashi’s insight and shares that it was precisely the unity, kinship, and love between all the members of Klal Yisrael which enabled them to receive the Torah on Har Sinai. 

What emerges from the above dichotomy is that ahavas Yisrael is the fertile soil through which Torah can sprout and grow. 

What is the relationship between ahavas Yisrael and reception of the Torah? 

In B’Yam Darkecha, a recent sefer from one of the talmidim of Rav Itche Meir Morgenstern on avodas Hashem, he writes in the first chapter on ahavas Yisrael that everything in creation is a vessel through which Hashem’s light is revealed (p. 17). 

The Ba’al B’Yam Darkecha explains that the essential avodah of ahavas Yisrael, therefore, is the capacity to perceive the neshama that animates every Yid (p. 18-19). The work is to gaze beyond the outer trappings of personality and idiosyncrasies and recognize the “spark of G-dliness” within that ultimately connects us all to Ha Kodesh Barchu. As the mechaber writes, “we are one neshama literally” (p. 18). 

Considering the above teaching from B’Yam Darkecha, I would like to suggest the following – the root of ahavas Yisrael is the ability to recognize that every Jew is truly a vehicle through which he or she expresses the light of Hashem. Therefore, through appreciating the light that abides in every Jew, a person then merits fixing and establishing the letters, words, sections, and halachos of Torah – the different units of expression – which then allow for the disclosure of Hashem’s light and, ultimately, Klal Yisrael’s capacity to receive the Torah. 

With Hashem’s help, may we see each other deeply, and in doing so, receive the Torah deeply. 

Gut Shabbos. 

Based on Hilchos Tefillas Mincha, Halachah ז,

Parashas Beshalach | Jan 15th 2022

No Fear

Rabbi David Yisrael Kalmus

I once had a conversation with a student who poured his heart to me about feeling genuinely trapped by his life’s circumstances. Constantly working in unfulfilling jobs which could not provide the basic needs of his family. Daily discord and dysfunction with his marriage partner and children. Intense dissatisfaction with his inability to make lasting progress in the area of the Brit or to find time for Hitbodedut, the practice of private secluded meditation which Rebbe Nachman extolled over all else (Likutey Moharan Tinyana 25). Across the board, he did not have one area of his life in which he felt remotely satisfied. 

I strongly encouraged him to take a time where he could be completely alone, without distractions or pressures, and muster up the courage to ask himself one fundamental question, “If I had no financial burdens, no marital issues with my spouse, no fears about public opinion or judgment of those closest to me, no limitations of time or resources, what would I want to spend my life doing?” 

He asked me why it matters if none of these circumstances applied to him. I proceeded to suggest that despite what appears to be uncontrollable, external factors being the cause of his discontent, the real reason he was not happy was because he was not living in harmony with his innermost will. And until he gave himself permission to cast aside all external fears and intrinsic doubts to recognize his deepest inner desire, he would always feel imprisoned by his circumstances. 

I concluded by stating that one’s true “ratzon,” will, must be the focal point of his or her life. Without constant cultivation, careful nurturing, and a perpetual moving towards this innermost “ratzon,” the experience of true joy and freedom will always feel out of reach (Likutey Moharan 22). 

This week’s Parashah, Beshalach, drives this essential point home. After the Jewish People had finally left slavery behind, their former Egyptian masters made one last ditch effort to prevent Klal Yisrael from achieving ultimate liberation. While being pursued aggressively and relentlessly from behind, Am Yisrael surged into the ocean with no assurance of survival. Through this unprecedented act of boldness, Paroh and the Mitzrim were drowned, and the Jewish People made their way to long-awaited freedom. 

When the Jewish People witnessed the miraculous reversal of fortune, they sang, “In Your love, You led this people and redeemed them, with Your boldness, you led them to your Divine abode” (Shemot 15:13). Rebbe Nachman expounds a powerful insight from the redemption song of our ancestors. It is only though “holy chutzpah,” unadulterated boldness, that one genuinely can enter into place of G-dliness (Likutey Moharan 22). 

The last thing most of us want to do is leave the comfort zone of what is considered socially normative and culturally acceptable. The issue is that this fear itself is handicapping us from experiencing that which we most deeply yearn for. If we could only dig down deep and operate from a place of uncompromising truth, we would finally find that thing which we have always been looking for. 

Freedom. 

“Know, that a person must cross a very, very narrow bridge in this world. And the main thing is not to fear at all” (Likutey Moharan Tinyana 48). 

Shabbat Shalom. 

On the Way, But Here Already 

Aaron S. London, RN, BSN 

Reb Noson from Nemirov, based on the first two pasukim in Parashas Beshalach, shares with us an insight into avodas Hashem that is as relevant today as it was when he wrote these words over 200 years ago in a small shtetl in the Ukraine. 

We learn from the beginning of the parashah that Hashem did not lead the Jewish people directly to Eretz Yisrael from Mitzrayim. Rather, as Rashi points out in pasuk יח, He led them on a circuitous route. Rashi explains in the previous pasuk, that if Hashem guided the people on a more direct pathway to Eretz Yisrael, they might succumb to thoughts of wanting to return to Mitzrayim. Why would they entertain such thoughts? Rashi comments that it would be easier for the Jewish people to return to Mitzrayim on a direct path than a non-direct path. 

Let us try to understand. As we have described in previous pieces, the Torah is not only conveying the historical narrative of the Jewish people. The Torah is also offering us insight into the development of the Jewish personality as a spiritual being in the physical world. Therefore, the reality of “Mitzrayim” exists on multiple planes. On the literal plane, it exists as the nation that enslaved the Israelites. On the psycho-spiritual plane, it exists as a state of consciousness. “Mitzrayim” shares the same etymological root as מצר which means “straits” or “constriction.” Consequently, “Mitzrayim” corresponds to what our sages call “constricted consciousness,” which connotes all iterations of unhealthy thinking. 

Eretz Yisrael, on the other hand, corresponds to “expanded consciousness” and connotes all iterations of healthy ways of looking at oneself and the world. In the language of Reb Noson based on the teachings of Rebbe Nachman, “Eretz Yisrael” is conceptually the same as emunah (faithfulness) and represents the journey towards what he describes as “berur hamidameh” – the refinement of the imagination. Said more succinctly, the ultimate refinement of one’s imagination is when one arrives at complete emunah. In contradistinction, indulging one’s proclivity towards fantasy draws a person away from emunah and drives him deeper into the space of the ego – the ultimate expression of “Mitzrayim,” where a person’s self-inflation occludes his ability to perceive G-dliness in his life. 

Herein lies Reb Noson’s important insight. One does not simply arrive at the land of Yisrael. As Reb Noson notes, a person needs to wander to many places prior to arriving in Eretz Yisrael. Or, said differently, a person does not simply arrive at emunah. He needs to journey towards emunah through the circuitous path Hashem leads him on, where each stop along the way provides the opportunity to re-frame one’s consciousness from a space of egoism to a space of faith. 

Indeed, there may creep up the desire to fall back into habituated, unhealthy ways of thinking. A person encounters the trials of daily living and wants to return to “Mitzrayim” so-to-speak, where it is easier to just get angry or frustrated rather than commit to rehabilitating the moment with a sense of emunah that this too is from Hashem. 

Nevertheless, as Reb Noson explains, Hashem wants us to travel to each and every place in our lives in order to redeem the “nitzotzai haemunah” – the sparks of faith – that have fallen there through our “bilbul hamidameh” – confused fantasies. 

But make no mistake. Even though a person has not yet arrived at the land of Yisrael – the state of mind called emunah – nevertheless, each and every step along the way offers the opportunity to experience that very step as another movement towards emunah. And, as Reb Joey speaks about in his shiurim, by virtue of one’s future arrival in the land of Yisrael and “emunah shlema,” a person actually experiences the present moment as if he has already arrived. 

(לקוטי הלכות, ברכת הריח וברכת הודאה ד, אות טז)

Gut Shabbos, 

Parashas Bo | Jan 7th-8th 2022

The Dark Knight 

Rabbi David Yisrael Kalmus  Refuah shlema for Linor bat Liora

One of the most beautiful aspects of Judaism that I have experienced since becoming Ba’al Teshuva is the deep, collective reverence and genuine appreciation of those who have sacrificed their lives for something greater than themselves. If you go into a Jewish bookstore, you will see the names of men and women who have achieved tremendous feats and seemingly impossible accomplishments. On the anniversary of the passing of these heroic individuals, Jews across the world celebrate their indelible contribution to the Jewish people and to humanity at large. However, in the process of contemplating the unprecedented impact of these true Tzaddikim, there is a certain natural vulnerability that wells up within each of us. 

“I will never be able to be like this person.” 

Following this instinctive response, there is a common grievous error made by the very best of us. “If this man or woman is so great, and his or her efforts cannot be replicated, then why should I even try to strive for spiritual greatness?” 

In this week’s Parashah, we receive a powerful reminder of why this self-deprecating internal commentary is not only personally destructive, but also inherently misguided. 

In Parashat Bo, Moshe Rabbeinu, the unparalleled spiritual dynamo, the preeminent prophet, and the generational leader par excellence, achieves the greatest feat in Jewish history. Through his sheer determination, unshakeable confidence, and spiritual mastery, Moshe rips the Jewish People out of a devastating servitude which lasted over two hundred years. In the common vernacular of 2022, he would be rightfully called the GOAT, “the Greatest Of All Time.” 

However, there is two unique instances where Moshe’s inherent greatness and incomparable mental clarity actually precluded his understanding of something that would only later be clarified by someone seemingly less exceptional. When Moshe initiated the final step of the Jewish People’s national redemption, the Torah states that Moshe had forewarned Paroh of the exact conditions in which the Jewish People would walk out of Mitzrayim. The departure, exclaimed Moshe Rabbeinu, would take place “k’chatzot,” around midnight. 

The Sages in the Gemara examine the unusual ambiguity of Moshe’s description of the time of departure. Why add “around” to the stated time of midnight? Just tell Paroh that the Jewish People will be leaving at midnight proper. The conclusion of our Sages is that Moshe did not know exactly when during the night he would take them out. He only knew in proximity (Brachot 3B). 

Additionally, when HaShem told Moshe the first Mitzvah that would ever be given to the Jewish People, the Mitzvah of Rosh Chodesh, Moshe had trouble recognizing the dimensions of the moon necessary for announcing the arrival of the new month (Rashi, Mechilta Shemot). 

On the other hand, our Sages noted that there was a person who was much less intellectually gifted and spiritually equipped than Moshe Rabbeinu, and yet this very person knew exactly when midnight commenced. Additionally, despite this person’s inherent lackings, he also possessed unique knowledge of the moon’s cyclical proclivities. This enigmatic figure was King David. 

King David spoke explicitly in Tehillim about his nightly routine of arising early to speak to HaShem in Hitbodedut, consistently waking up at “Chatzot,” midnight (Tehillim 119). 

David did not wake up around midnight. It was midnight exactly (Brachot 3). 

Additionally, the first time that the celebration of Rosh Chodesh is mentioned in the Torah is by King David himself, when he told his best friend Yehonatan, “Behold, tomorrow is Rosh Chodesh” (Shmuel I 20:5)! 

What is it about the darkness of night time and about the unique nature of the moon that was so difficult for Moshe to grasp? And why was King David so oddly attuned to these very same matters? 

Rebbe Nachman’s main disciple, Rav Natan, states in his magnum opus, Likutey Halachot, that the entire reason that David understood what Moshe could not, was because for one to truly understand night time, one must be able to thrive without Da’at, spiritual clarity (Likutey Halachot, Orach Chaim, Hashkamat HaBoker). 

The AriZal, the preeminent Kabbalistic master, states in his profound writings that Moshe Rabbeinu was the living manifestation of Da’at. His entire life was the conscious, felt, lived experience of HaShem being intimately involved in every aspect of his existence. Therefore, since Moshe was Da’at itself, he had no idea what it was like to function without it. He saw HaShem “face to face.” It was always day time for Moshe. 

David, on the other hand, lived a life without such penetrating clarity. In fact, David had no intrinsic light of his own at all. (Zohar Vayishlach) His normative experience was that of constant “running and returning,” rising up and falling down, ascending and descending. In this way, David mirrored the moon itself (Likutey Moharan 1). For King David, it was always nighttime. 

Paradoxically, it was King David’s constant struggles and acute suffering which gave him unique insights regarding the different phenomenon of nighttime, insights which eluded Moshe almost entirely. 

But can you imagine if David grew up in 2022. He would read of the great feats of his wondrous predecessor, Moshe Rabbienu, and simply ask, “What is the point of even trying? I will never been like him. In fact, I am nothing like him at all.” And David would have missed out on the entire greatness that was unique to his life. The incomprehensible resilience to overcome every trial and tribulation that came his way. 

The undying courage to keep getting back up, no matter how many times he fell. The insane chutzpah to lead his entire people on Emunah alone! 

And you know the most ironic part? In the end, the Mashiach does not come from the otherworldly brilliance of Moshe Rabbeinu. The Final Redeemer of Klal Yisrael comes from the dark knight himself, King David. 

The final chapter of history will be one in which the light of the moon, King David, will be shown to illuminate as bright as that the of the sun itself, Moshe Rabbeinu. In fact, even a little brighter. This secret is hinted to by King David’s son, Shlomo HaMelech, when he states, “A woman of valor (King David) is her husband’s (Moshe Rabbeinu) crown” (Mishlei 12:4). 

I exhort each of us that we should reflect deeply on our lives and ask ourselves the hard question. Have we given up our own personal share in this world because it seemed to pale in comparison to the great ones before and around us? If so, do a double take. Because everything about you, your strengths and your vulnerabilities, your yearnings and your failings, your waxing and your waning, could all be exactly what the world needs. 

Shabbat Shalom 

Awake within the Dream 

Aaron S. London, RN, BSN

Rabbi Shmuel Silber, in his series of shiurim on Rav Tzaddok’s Tzidkas HaTzaddik, draws our attention to the two foundational modes of experience that R’ Tzaddok explains in seifim gimmel and dalet. These two states of being are rooted in the language of Shema – u-v’shawch b’cha uv-ku-me-cha – when you lie down and when you get up. In other words, when a person is awake and conscious and when a person is asleep and unconscious. 

The point R’ Tzaddok makes in these two seifim is that the mitzvah of kabbalos ol malchus shamayim (the essential mitzvah of Shema) – accepting upon oneself the obligation to serve Hashem – applies whether one is awake or asleep. 

Seif gimmel, as R’ Silber elucidates, refers to the literal understanding of conscious and unconscious. Ultimately, the way in which a person spends his conscious time influences what emerges when a person dreams in his sleep state. Where the mind goes when it is not subject to conscious thought reveals a certain understanding of where that person is truly holding in his spiritual development. Therefore, we have a mitzvah to say Shema when we lie down and when we get up. That is to say, kabbalos ol malchus shamayim should saturate even the dreams of a person’s sleep experience. 

In seif dalet, R’ Tzaddok explores why the first mitzvah of a bar mitzvah bachur is krias shema shel arvis (the Shema of maariv). He excavates more deeply the concept of darkness which is associated with u-v’shawch-b’cha. R’ Tzaddok explains that the key message is as follows: the bar mitzvah bachur’s first mitzvah is krias shema shel arvis because he has to learn to accept ol malchus shamayim even in darkness. That is to say, when a person’s awareness of G-d’s presence is impoverished, whether that is through some form personal difficulty or some other trial or tribulation, nevertheless, he must accept upon himself that Hashem is with him. 

Perhaps, the aforementioned dynamic between being asleep and being awake can also be understood in the context of galus and ga’ula. The climax of this week’s parashah is the Jewish people’s redemption from Mitzrayim. 

Our sages teach us that galus and ga’ula exist not only on a national-historic level, but on a psycho-spiritual level as well. 

The point I would like to emphasize emerges from our discussion regarding R’ Tzaddok’s teaching. Indeed, we all experience the spiritual states of u-v’shawch-b’cha uv-ku-me cha. We move into sleep and shift into wakefulness, progressing from the darkness of galus to the light of ga’ula. 

Herein lies the point: when we understand that kabbalos ol malchus shamayim exists even in darkness, whatever expression that darkness takes, then we reach the ga’ula that lives within the galus and we flow into the experience of wakefulness even while being asleep. 

Indeed, as we await our final redemption and the complete state of G-d consciousness, we can strengthen ourselves with the avodah of u-v’shawch-b’cha and experience being awake even within the dream. 

Gut Shabbos, 

ALY 

P.S. Although I do not directly quote R’ Joey, this piece is no doubt influenced by his Torah. 

Parashas Va’eira | Dec 31st / Jan 1 2022

What Did You Accomplish? 

Rabbi David Yisrael Kalmus 

When Rebbe Nachman was thirty years old, he moved to the city of Breslov. It was there that he attracted a large number of students and disciples. However, as his Chassidim came to understand fairly quickly, to have any type of relationship with Rebbe Nachman came with tremendous resistance. The closer the relationship to the Rebbe, the greater the resistance. The greatest of which came from the vehement opposition of Rebbe Nachman’s very own peers. 

The Baal Shem Tov, Rebbe Nachman’s great-grandfather and the forebear of Chassidus, drew enmity from those who didn’t have the merit to taste the sweetness of his novel approach to experiencing genuine closeness with HaShem. These enemies 

are historically known as “Mitnagdim,” opposers of the Baal Shem Tov and Chassidus in general. While this would be enough of a challenge for any future Chassid to contend with, Rebbe Nachman drew the ire not only of the “Mitnagdim,” the opposers of Chassidus, but of the other factions of Chassidim themselves! 

Under the weight of this unparalleled and undeserved hostility, Rebbe Nachman’s students felt quite heavy and rightfully so. That was all until their first Shabbat Chanukah in Breslov with the Rebbe. 

There were three times a year that Rebbe Nachman exhorted his disciples to be with him, without exception. These established times were Rosh HaShana, Shavuot, and Shabbat Chanukah. When the disciples of Rebbe Nachman arrived in Breslov for Shabbat Chanukah, they opened up to their Rebbe about the harsh and unfair criticism being directed towards them. The main source of torment was from a fellow Jew in the nearby town of Nemirov who had been falsely persecuting the Breslover Chassidim. 

Rebbe Nachman responded immediately, as he was known to do, by delivering an ingenious lesson dealing with the specific challenges brought up by his students, intricately weaving their vexation and concerns into a novel and comprehensive Torah lesson about life (Likutey Moharan 8). Rebbe Nachman told his Chassidim afterwards, “Should you be asked what you accomplished here in Breslov, tell them Ruach!” (Chayei Moharan 130) 

What is so powerful about, “ruach,” breath, that it should have allayed the troubles of Rebbe Nachman’s faithful students? What is it about “ruach” that should allow us 210 years later to deal with the frenetic challenges of modern life? The answer can be found in this week’s Parashah, Parashat Va’eira. 

When HaShem asked Moshe Rabbeinu to take the Jewish People out of Mitzrayim, he responded, “But they will not listen to me.” After tremendous encouragement, Moshe entered the heart of exile to tell his suffering brethren that redemption was coming. The Torah states that they could not hear Moshe because of “kotzer ruach,” shortness of breath. Not that Moshe’s message was not transformative or novel. They simply could not make out what Moshe was saying because they could not catch their breath. 

The Zohar compares the Tzaddik, the spiritual master of the generation, to Shabbat. Shabbat is a time of deep, restorative rest. This is a quality of rest that is not offered by the modern world. However, to access the tranquility and ecstasy of Shabbat is not as simple as turning off your phone and television. It first requires a deep breath. 

Paroh and the Mitzrim worked the Jews to the pulp and, as a result, they could not hear the answer to their lifelong distress. 

So too, modern life and society have relegated the only message of true comfort completely inaudible to the modern Jewish ear, secular and religious alike. 

And herein lies the the powerful message of Rebbe Nachman. What is this great spiritual master offering in Breslov that is practically non-existent elsewhere? 

Ruach. 

The ability to take a deep breath. 

And with this breath alone, Rebbe Nachman explains that one draws life force into each and everyone of his or her lackings. It is no surprise then that modern psychology utilizes deep breathing, especially with its most acutely pained clients, prior to any type of therapeutic intervention. Without this deep breath, they “cannot hear” the wisdom or advice needed to come out of their challenges. 

But rather than give a temporary panacea to deep rooted suffering, Rebbe Nachman teaches us how to have the ability to breath deeply always. We do this through his innovative approach to daily secluded meditation, known as Hitbodedut. We do this through his unprecedented wisdom and comprehensive advice given on every situation and challenge that we come across in our lives. We do this through the echoes of his roar of unmitigated hope in the face of all trials and tribulations. 

Rebbe Nachman teaches one how to breath. And in doing so, we can finally hear our inner voice telling us what it has been silently screaming all along. 

Redemption is coming. 

And if you are like me, and like any of the students of Rebbe Nachman before me, than you have also faced your own share of unwarranted criticism and cynicism. Whether these attacks levied against you are primarily external or even deeply internal, there is only one real way to respond to questions about the legitimacy and potency of Breslov Chassidus and its Rebbe. 

Take a deep breath. 

Then tell them Ruach! 

Shabbat Shalom 

Avodah Chaburah 

Thoughts and practices in Avodas Hashem Based on R’ Moshe Weinberger’s shiurim on sefer Binei Machshava Tova of the Piaseczna Rebbe and other sourcesThe world is composed of constant miracles the eye is accustomed to seeing. Avodas Hashem begins with stopping and seeing the miracle within teva itself (R’ Weinberger). 

Based on the first Torah in sefer Likutey Moharan, a person needs humility in order to perceive the miracle at the heart of teva. One of the key dimensions of humility is the willingness to say, “Hashem, You are in control and everything You send my way is there to help me grow.” At that moment, teva is transformed and Hashem demonstrates that the concealment itself is a revelation of spiritual light (R’ Joey based on the Leshem). 

Then, I can perceive even the concealment as a miracle. 

Gut Shabbos, 

ALY

Parashas Shemos | Dec 24th-25th 2021

Exile Ends with Faith

The Torah is not a history book. Its not even a religious doctrine. The Torah is the essential psycho-spiritual guide to inner transformation. No where is that more evident than in the second of the five books of the Torah which we are beginning this Shabbos, Sefer Shemot. 

Parshat Shemot is a stunningly comprehensive treatise on the exile of one’s true self. How does one become lost in life? What events take place along the way that deepen the loss of one’s essential self over time? Why does a person have to grapple with exile in the first place? And finally, what’s the catalyst that pushes one to ultimately find him or herself? All of these questions are thoroughly examined in Parshat Shemot. 

The answer to all of these questions are to be found in the seventh lesson of Likutey Moharan. There, Rebbe Nachman concludes that the cause of all personal and collective exile begins and ends with two haunting words, “chesron b’emunah,” a lack of faith. It is the lack of conviction in one’s core beliefs that cause him or her to be exiled. Nothing more, nothing less. 

Rebbe Nachman was once presenting a powerful discourse on the root cause of heaviness in one’s daily life. Rebbe Nachman concluded that to the degree that one lacks belief, to that degree everything in his life feels heavy. 

In hearing this, Rav Natan, the main disciple of Rebbe Nachman, became visibly upset. Contemplating the heaviness of his own life and the inordinate difficulty with which each task in his day required, Rav Natan blurted out in pain and confusion, “But if there is one thing I have, it is faith!” His Rebbe responded, “It is true. You believe in HaShem. But you do not believe in yourself.” 

The exile has never been more palpable or our lives more heavy than they are right now. Rebbe Nachman predicted this explicitly over two hundred years ago. But we must understand that the way we came in is the same way we must go out. Exile began with a lack of belief. Redemption will begin with a blossoming of belief. And no belief is more fundamental to our generation than the belief in one’s self. 

I remember a very intense session of Hitbodedut I had while living in New York a few years ago. I had put away my smart phone along with all other possible distractions and entered the field. Feeling the heaviness of life, I poured my heart out to HaShem. As I was reaching the end of my daily, hour-long conversation with HaShem, I came to a startling realization. My emotional pain was not coming from those around me. It was not even coming from the intense challenges I had been presented with in my life. It was all due to the fact that I did not really believe in myself. 

Ever since I had this epiphany, a day has not gone by that I have not prayed to HaShem to be able to truly believe in myself. That I am good. That I am capable. That I have the strength to rise above my inherent lackings. That I have a mission in this world that is real and meaningful, and that I must pursue it at all costs. As a result of this daily effort, I have felt a degree of freedom even before redemption has truly arrived. 

I bless each of us to be able to take Rebbe Nachman’s most emphatic advice. To take a time alone each day to cultivate one’s belief in HaShem. One’s belief in His Torah. One’s belief in True Tzaddikim. And perhaps most importantly, the belief in one’s self. 

Shabbat Shalom.

Dancing with Hope

Aaron London, RN, BSN

We danced round and round in circles as if the world had done no wrong 

From evening until morning, filling up the shul with song Though we had no Sifrei Torah to clutch close to our hearts In their place we held the future of a past so torn apart. 

Such are the words from Abie Rotenberg’s composition, “A Man from Vilna,” which describes the encounter between the narrator and a Holocaust survivor as they share a plane ride together. The survivor, on his way back from a wedding in Chicago, invites the narrator into the experience of his return to Vilna at that time of liberation in 1944/1945. 

As the survivor and the chevra he was with enter the city, one of them realizes that Simchas Torah was that night. 

The survivor recounts, “We ran as one towards the shul, our spirits in a trance / And we tore apart the barricade, in defiance we would dance/ But the scene before our eyes shook us to the core / Scraps of siddur, bullet holes, bloodstains on the floor.” 

They confront not only the rubble of a broken shul, but also the Aron Kodesh bereft of its Sifrei Torah. 

However, amongst the debris, they discover two crying children, the only children present amongst the survivors. 

The survivor continues, “We danced round and round in circles as if the world had done no wrong / From evening until morning, filling up the shul with song / Though we had no Sifrei Torah to clutch and hold up high / In their place we held those children, Am Yisrael Chai.” 

R’ Joey Rosenfeld, in his series of shiurim on hope, describes the following concept based on the 78th teaching in sefer Likutey Moharan, Section Seven: “the hope within hopelessness itself” (Hope 9: Rebbe Nachman – Hope at the Heart of Hopelessness). 

Upon an initial glance, “the hope within hopelessness” strikes us as a paradoxical concept. How can there be hope in the place of no hope? In answering this question, R’ Joey draws our attention to the seeming contradiction between two statements Rebbe Nachman makes in Torah 78. At the beginning of section seven, Rebbe Nachman explains, “The rule is: It is forbidden to despair” (p. 81, Volume 15 in BRI printing). The assumption is that a person can indeed fall into despair, however, there is an isur not to. Later on, Reb Noson documents the Rebbe as exclaiming with a power that has echoed throughout the generations, “Kein yiush iz gor nit fahr-handin!” – “there is no such thing as despair!” (p. 83). The assumption in the later statement is that despair does not even exist as a reality. 

Herein lies the depth: when we turn our gaze towards the Aron Kodesh, we hope to see the Sifrei Torah behind the veil. When we look towards the world, we hope to experience the light of Hashem behind the darkness. When we peer into ourselves, we hope to perceive the glow of the neshama behind all the trials of being. 

And then, there is that horrifying moment, when we see that the Sifrei Torah are gone, and the world remains dark, and even within ourselves we cannot apprehend the inner spark G-dliness. 

We encounter hopelessness itself. And yet, in the next moment, the children cry out from the rubble. We look again at the world and realize we are still capable of looking. If we are capable of looking, we are capable of living. If we are capable of living, that means our neshamos burn inside of us. With our neshamos burning inside of us, hope then energizes our existence. 

The survivors did not take out the Sifrei Torah from the Aron Kodesh that Simchas Torah night. Rather, from the carnage of the chorben, they pulled out children – alive and breathing and danced throughout the night with hope itself.

With Hashem’s help, may we also dance throughout our days and nights, carrying with us the hope that is always present. 

Gut Shabbos, 

ALY (Aryeh Leib Yishaya)

Parashas Vayechi | Dec 17th-18th 2021

Father and Son

Rabbi David Yisrael Kalmus (Dedicated to my father for his Refua Shlema, Avraham Ben Sarah Esther, and an Aliyah of the Neshama for Zecharia Yosef Yisrael Ben Moshe Yitzhak) 

As we come to our conclusion of the first book of the Torah, something quite beautiful is coming into focus. To truly grasp this beauty, we must first remember a principle transmitted by our Sages. The unfolding of spiritual reality, paralleled exactly by the unfolding of physical reality, hinges on a unique phenomenon known as “The end is wedged in the beginning.” This foundational principle is teaching us that the end of any process must faithfully reflect the original purpose for the process itself. 

For example, when an architect is hired to create a world-class structure, he begins by meditating on the purpose of the structure. Only then does he begin to formulate ideas which could give birth to that desired goal. Once the idea has been concretized, then the architect draws up a blueprint. From there, construction workers are hired to build this structure from the ground up. 

From the beginning of construction until the end, the original purpose of the structure becomes obscured by the intensive labor taking place. Only once the building is finalized does the structure actually shine with the original purpose and vision for which it was created. 

So too, our world is in a delicate period in which the purpose of its being created is deeply obscured. In fact, according to Rebbe Nachman, we are reaching a new point in history where the true meaning of our lives is doubly concealed from us. But through utilizing the principle of “The end is wedged in the beginning”, we can still make out the ultimate destination of this challenging and unique time period. 

The Torah began with “In the beginning, HaShem created the spiritual and physical universe”. In the final chapter of the first book of the Torah, Parshat Vayechi, we learn about the conclusion of the lives of Yaakov Avinu and his beloved son Yosef. 

What’s the inherent connection between HaShem originally creating time and space, and the ultimate recounting of the final moments of the lives of Yaakov and Yosef? 

The answer is that HaShem created the world for one purpose alone. That purpose was not to become wealthy or famous. It was not to chase after selfish motives or to embrace nihilism. 

The purpose of everything was to cultivate a relationship between a son and his father. 

Our Sages teach, “One is obligated to say that the whole world was created just for me”. Rebbe Nachman adds that while its true that the world was created just for me, it is only in order that I should find Him. 

Growing up, my father and I spent a lot of time together. We shared a love of sports and classic rock. My father was good at sports. I was bad at them. My father was a Paul McCartney fan. I was a John Lennon fan. My father liked The Who. I was obsessed with Led Zeppelin. One song that we both loved however is called “Father and Son” by Cat Stevens. 

“I was once like you are now, and I know that it’s not easy. You’re still young. That’s your fault. There’s so much you have to go through. All the times that I’ve cried, keeping all the things I knew inside. Now there’s a way, and I know, I have to go away.”

The dynamic of father and son is so poignant and yet so complicated. Its full of love, but at times indescribably painful. Their personal journey’s leave them estranged at periods, yet they remain inextricably connected. The inner yearnings of both father and son are inherently good, but the events of their lives fuddle those innate desires. 

However, just as the purpose of the world can only be found at the end of it, so too the true relationship of father and son can only be fully appreciated at the end. The relationship of Yaakov and his son Yosef reflects the unique relationship HaShem has with each of us. 

It begins with a special love. That love prompts the father to send his son away to check on “his brothers”. Along the way, he is sold and enslaved, alienated from his family and society. Through the memory of his father and the courage of his conviction alone, he makes it out alive. Along the way, he finds genuine healing and eternal strength for all his father’s children. Afterwards, father and son finally reunite in an emotional, teary eyed embrace. And the purpose of their personal journeys and painful periods of separation finally weave into one exquisite tapestry. A tapestry that testifies to the ultimate truth. That the son and father are really one, and therefore had never left each other to begin with. 

I bless each of us to have the courage, the patience, and the resilience to see this thing through till the end. To continue searching for Him and His love for you even when the events of your lives point to the contrary. To keep fighting until father and son are shown to be one. 

There is a famous saying that frequented the lips of my Rebbe, Rav Walkin Ztl, as tears would well up in his eyes, “The final chapter has yet to be written!” With HaShem’s help, we should see it written very soon. Until then, hold on. 

Shabbat Shalom 

Emunah at the Heart of Imperfection 

Aaron London, RN, BSN 

One of the foundational concepts that can be learned from the lives of our Avos and Imos is the concept of emunah- emunah that is forged from within imperfection and difficulty and the 

daily trials of what it means to be a human being in Olam Ha’zeh where the light of spirituality can so often feel imperceptible. Avraham endures ten tests. Yitzchak is nearly killed by his father. Yaakov lives for years in the home of his father-in-law who takes every opportunity to exploit him. Yehudah is intimate with Tamar who poses as a prostitute. The list continues. The lives of our forebearers were not lives of perfection. Living a G-dly life is not equated to living a perfect life. Living a G-dly life is about having emunah that one’s imperfect life is perfectly placed within Hashem’s plan, as the title of Rabbi Elimelech Goldberg’s book on helping kids with cancer – A Perfect G-d Created an Imperfect World Perfectly – suggests. 

At the core of their experiences is the awareness that Hashem is right there, as is most potently expressed in last week’s parashah when Yosef tells his brothers after revealing himself to them, “So now it was not you who sent me here, but G-d” (45:8). 

Rebbe Nachman offers us an insight into living with emunah. Rebbe Nachman teaches in the 4th Torah in sefer Likutey Maharan the concept of “borrowing from the future.” 

The Rebbe references the Gemara is Pescahim 50a, which explains, “At present the blessing ‘Who is good and beneficent’ is recited over good, whereas, the ‘truthful Judge’ is recited over bad. But in the Future, it will be entirely ‘Who is good and beneficent.’ The holy name Y[K]V[K] amd the holy name Elo[k]im will be totally one” (p. 117, Volume 1, BRI printing). 

In other words, a person can gaze at Olam Ha’zeh with eyes of Olam Ha’bah. By virtue of the fact that it will be good, a person can actually see things as good right now and learn to make a space inside for whatever difficulty has come his way.

The aforementioned point is the secret of emunah that has sustained the Jewish people throughout time. Perhaps, I cannot comprehend how whatever I am going through right now is good. However, by knowing that it will good, I can strengthen myself in the belief that it is also good right now. In so doing, I experience the imperfection of the human experience as precisely the place where emunah is grown.

Parashas Vayigash | Dec10th-11th 2021

The Greatest Comfort 

Rabbi David Yisrael Kalmus

In Parashat Vayigash, an epic confrontation takes place between two of the most compelling figures in the Torah. Yehuda, the courageous and unquestioned leader of the Children of Yaakov, aggressively approaches Yosef, the charismatic and dynamic younger brother who’s life had inexplicably transformed from that of intense personal suffering and servitude to that of unparalleled spiritual mastery and universal influence. 

The most gripping part of this showdown is that Yehuda does not actually know he is speaking to Yosef, for he had not seen his younger brother in 17 years. Instead, Yehuda thought he was speaking to the harsh and unsympathetic viceroy of a foreign kingdom. At the apex of Yehuda’s frustration, he even told Yosef he was like “Pharaoh,” the ruthless militant leader of an unjust society. 

At the very same time, Yosef knew exactly who he was speaking to. As the Torah states regarding this unusual dynamic, “Yosef recognized his brothers, but his brothers did not recognize him.” 

Following the impassioned pleading of Yehuda, Yosef had to forcibly remove himself from the conversation. Due to the aching pain welling up in Yosef’s heart at the sight of his brother’s distress, Yosef excused himself to a private room where he proceeded to weep with great intensity. Afterwards, Yosef washed his face and came back out to continue his charade of indifference. 

This mysterious back and forth is something our Sages go to great lengths to explain. However, it was not until my late Rabbi Aharon Walkin Ztl revealed something to me that made me realize the life changing depth of this entire interaction. 

Based on a powerful Midrash, Rav Walkin explained that Yosef composed himself as a harsh and distant authority figure only to afford his brothers the opportunity to achieve genuine teshuva. Iwas an act rooted in the ultimate level of empathy. One in whichno one else would be capable of carrying out, as it required the 

deepest level of maturity, emotional awareness, and genuine selflessness to perform. For without this external facade on the part of Yosef, his brothers would not have been able to rectify the egregious error they made two decades earlier in exiling Yosef from his own home and estranging him from the only family he ever knew. 

The fundamental point Rav Walkin added to this Midrash, and one in which Rebbe Nachman similarly expounds on as well, is that just as Yosef is the archetypal “Tzaddik Yesod Olam,” the 

central figure on whom the entire world stands, he is only a mere reflection and window into the ultimate “Tzaddik Yesod Olam,” HaShem himself. That is to say, that the entire drama between Yosef and his brothers is really an exact parallel to the drama currently unfolding between HaShem and us. 

Therefore, the painful experiences we have all endured in our lives, the private grudges we have developed and continue to harbor, and the heartfelt pleading we have since engaged in withHaShem, are all reflected by Yehuda approaching Yosef. 

HaShem’s seeming “indifference” to our plight is really nothing other than the rich soil from which our individual heroism will ultimately blossom. HaShem’s ability to withhold his true intentions and feelings, are paradoxically His greatest compassion.

But be sure of this. Just as Yehuda before us, if we refuse to give up and continuously approach Him, one day soon we will also get to hear the truth. 

“I’m Yosef.” 

And in the meantime, while we are trying to muster up the courage to continue fighting, remember and meditate deeply on this point. 

While you are in distress, HaShem is not just listening. He is also crying with you. 

This is actually the greatest comfort of all. 

Shabbat Shalom.

Ga’ula at the Heart of Galus

Aaron London, RN, BSN

Reb Yossi Katz, in his sefer The Rebbe’s Shabbos Table, shares with us the following teaching based on the writings of Reb Nosson of Breslov in Likutey Halachos, Yoreh Deah, Hilchos Shluach HaKen, Halachah Heh, Sections 23-24: Yaakov decides to sojourn to Mitzrayim (Egypt) after learning that Yosef is still alive. Prior to his departure, Hashem says to him, “I will go down with you to Egypt, and I will also bring you up…” (46:4). The concept of “going down to Mitzrayim” does not just mean in a physical sense. Rather, as Reb Yossi explains, “going down to Mitzrayim” conveys the notion of Yaakov’s descent into exile and the resulting trepidation he felt (p. 69). Mitzrayim comes from the language of constriction and, therefore, on the level of penimiyus, the Torah is teaching us that Yaakov was moving from the expanded experience of self represented by Eretz Yisroel to the exiled experience of self represented by Mitzrayim. Reb Nosson writes towards the beginning of section 23 that the essential expression of galus Yisroel is the galus hanefesh. He explains, “All ascensions and descentions that occur to a Jewish man is the essential secret of galus (exile) and ga’ula (redemption)… which is the concept of a descent for the sake of an ascent” (p. 286). Therefore, R’ Nosson’s reading of the aforementioned pasuk teaches us that galus / descension is the necessary groundwork for ga’ula / ascension. 

At the heart of the above teaching is a paradigm that I often share with the people I work with in substance abuse. It is a paradigm that I myself have been working for many years to 

inculcate into my being and this paradigm emerges out of the following question: when it comes to emotional and psychological well-being, how do we relate to our inner worlds? How do we relate to ourselves when we experience the inevitable “lows” of daily living? Do we fester negative feelings towards ourselves? Is there guilt? Do we harbor residual feelings that blunt our ability to move forward? Or, alternatively, do we recognize that ebbs and flows are intrinsic to the human experience? If we understand that ebbs and flows are part and parcel to what it means to be human, then the gift that we offer ourselves is the gift of buoyancy and fluidity anchored in our acknowledgment that true growth involves ups and downs. 

One of my teachers shared with me the following metaphor which I believe captures the essence of the idea. Imagine that there are two people standing on a beach. The waves pull one person into the ocean, while the other person is able to stay grounded in the sand. What is the difference between these two people? Not that one person is experiencing the waves and the other is not. They both are experiencing the waves. Rather, the key difference is that one is able to stabilize himself in the presence of the water, while the other is not. 

The reason this metaphor is profound is because it conveys that mental heath does not mean someone is perfect without issues. Rather, the true barometer of mental health is a person’s ability to make a space for the waves of his inner world. Do these waves overwhelm me or is my sense of self bigger than the waves themselves? Herein lies the depth of R’ Nosson’s teaching. When I understand that my experience of galus, in whatever expression that takes, is not reflective of something wrong with me, but rather the fertile soil for my ultimately ga’ula, then I have learned the secret of how to stay standing on the beach. 

At that point, a person no longer has to be afraid because he has transformed his relationship to the experience of galus itself. 

Galus, therefore, is not something to run away from. Rather, together with Hashem, we walk into galus only to discover that the derech to ga’ula is traversed specifically through the vulnerability and courage that galus engenders. 

Gut Shabbos, 

ALY
